month.title: React + TypeScript
month.theme: Build component-based interfaces with predictable state and types, the way most product teams build today.
month.mastery: Explain component architecture and state flow.
month.checkpoint: A typed React app with reusable components and a written explanation of where state lives and why.

weeks.title: React fundamentals
weeks.objective: Think in components: break a UI into pieces, pass data down with props, and render lists.
learn: Why React: UI as a function of state
Vite: creating and running a React project
React DevTools: inspecting the component tree
practice: Take a Figma screen you designed and draw its component tree on paper
Build a Card component and render 6 cards from an array
Show an empty state when the array is empty
Inspect your tree in React DevTools

build.title: Contact list, rebuilt in React
build.brief: Rebuild your Week 6 contact list in React with components: App, ContactForm, ContactList, ContactCard, TagFilter. Compare the two codebases.

weeks.prove: Draw the component tree and props for your app from memory, then check it against React DevTools.
reflect: What got easier in React compared with plain DOM code, and what got more confusing?
weeks.ship: React contact list on GitHub with a component diagram in the README.

tryFirst.task: Render a list of contacts as cards, with a fallback message if there are none.
tryFirst.hint: Arrays have a method that turns each item into something else. Every item in a rendered list needs a stable key.
tryFirst.explanation: JSX lets you map data into elements. Keys tell React which item is which between renders, so use a stable id rather than the array index when items can be reordered or deleted.

weeks.title: Components and state
weeks.objective: Decide where state lives, lift it when siblings need it, and derive everything else.
learn: Lifting state up to a common parent
Derived state: compute it, don't store it
Immutable updates for arrays and objects
practice: Build a counter, then a toggle, then a tabs component
Lift a search query so a SearchBox and a List can share it
Replace a stored 'filteredItems' with a derived value
Refactor one large component into three

build.title: Habit tracker
build.brief: Track a few habits across the week: add habits, tick off days, and see a streak per habit. Decide deliberately where each piece of state lives and write it down.

weeks.prove: Explain, with a diagram, where every piece of state in your habit tracker lives and why.
reflect: Which piece of state did you store that you could have derived?
weeks.ship: Habit tracker on GitHub with a 'state map' in the README.

tryFirst.task: A SearchBox and a ResultList are siblings. Typing in the SearchBox should filter the ResultList.
tryFirst.hint: Siblings can't talk to each other directly. Find their closest common parent.
tryFirst.explanation: Lift the query into the parent. Pass the value and a setter down to SearchBox, and pass the filtered list (derived during render) down to ResultList. One source of truth.

weeks.title: Forms, events and data
weeks.objective: Build forms that validate, guide and recover, and load and save data without spaghetti.
learn: Accessible forms: labels, and errors linked with aria-describedby
useEffect: synchronising with things outside React, and when not to use it
Fetching data in React: loading, error, success
practice: Build a sign-up form whose inline errors only appear after the field loses focus
Fetch a list in a component with a loading skeleton and a retry button
Find one useEffect you can delete

build.title: Habit tracker: forms, editing and persistence
build.brief: Add create and edit forms with validation, persistence across refresh, and an import of starter habits from a JSON file. Every async path has a visible state.

weeks.prove: Break your own form: empty input, very long input, emoji, pasted spaces, double submit. Fix what fails and list the cases in the README.
reflect: When did you reach for useEffect, and did you actually need it?
weeks.ship: Updated habit tracker deployed (Vercel, Netlify or GitHub Pages).

tryFirst.task: Build a controlled email input that shows 'Enter a valid email' only after the user leaves the field.
tryFirst.hint: You need two pieces of state: the value, and whether the field has been touched. The error itself is derived.
tryFirst.explanation: Showing errors while someone is still typing is hostile. Track 'touched' on blur, derive the error from the value, and connect the message to the input with aria-describedby so screen readers hear it.

weeks.title: TypeScript fundamentals
weeks.objective: Use types to make impossible states impossible and let the compiler catch bugs before users do.
learn: Why types: catching mistakes while you write
Basic types, arrays, objects, optional properties
Discriminated unions for loading, success and error
practice: Type your contact and habit data shapes
Model a request as a discriminated union and switch on it
Turn on strict mode and fix every error
Find one real bug the compiler caught

build.title: Habit tracker in TypeScript
build.brief: Convert the habit tracker to TypeScript with strict mode on. No 'any' for app data. Model async data as a discriminated union.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: build a small React + TypeScript app and explain its component architecture and state flow.
reflect: Which bug would TypeScript have caught in your earlier projects?
weeks.ship: TypeScript habit tracker on GitHub, with your architecture explanation in the README.

tryFirst.task: Model a data request that can be idle, loading, loaded with data, or failed with a message, so that it is impossible to read the data while it is loading.
tryFirst.hint: Instead of several booleans, use one 'status' field, and let each status carry only the fields that make sense for it.
tryFirst.explanation: A discriminated union shares a literal 'status' field. After you check status === 'success', TypeScript knows data exists. Booleans such as isLoading plus isError allow nonsense combinations; a union doesn't.

mastery.title: Explain component architecture and state flow
mastery.challenge: Build a small React + TypeScript app from a blank Vite project (a reading list, a moodboard organiser, a client-brief checklist), then explain its architecture.
constraints: Start from an empty Vite template, not a starter kit
No tutorial for this app; React and TypeScript docs are allowed
AI may review your code after you've written it, not write it
criteria: At least 5 components with clear responsibilities
Strict TypeScript, no 'any' for app data
State lives in the right place, and derived values aren't stored
Async or persisted data has explicit loading and error states
A component and state diagram you drew yourself
You can explain what re-renders when a user types, and why
